name: Kerokan

card.summary: Kerokan is the Indonesian form of coin-scraping in which a smooth edge is rubbed over oiled skin until red streaks appear, used for relaxation and as a home remedy and sometimes alongside facial gua sha routines for a refreshed look.
card.aka: Indonesian gua sha, coin rubbing, cạo gió (Vietnamese counterpart)
card.note: Leaves red or purple marks that can be mistaken for injury; skin trauma and infection are possible with unclean tools.

quick.overview:
Kerokan is a traditional Indonesian practice in which the back, neck or shoulders are rubbed with a coin or similar blunt object, usually over oil or balm, until red streaks show. Practitioners use it for the feeling of relief and warmth it gives, particularly when feeling unwell or tired.

It is the Indonesian counterpart of gua sha, whose facial version has been promoted on social media for a smoother, de-puffed look. Kerokan itself is mostly a body practice; its appearance link is mainly through that broader scraping culture and the visible marks it leaves. Published work on it is mostly case reports and qualitative studies.
quick.how: People apply oil or balm to the skin and draw a coin, ginger piece or similar blunt edge in repeated strokes, commonly on the back and neck, until red lines appear. It is usually done at home or by a family member, and the marks are said to fade over several days.
quick.risks: It nearly always leaves redness or bruising, and blisters, abrasions and infection from unclean tools are possible. A 2020 forensic case report described how kerokan marks around the neck prompted a police investigation. A qualitative study of Indonesian breast cancer patients found some used kerokan for breast pain while delaying medical care.

lead: Kerokan (literally "scraping") is the Indonesian name for a folk practice in which a blunt object such as a coin or a piece of ginger is rubbed over the skin, typically with oil, to produce red streaks [1][3]. It is considered the Indonesian counterpart of gua sha, the East Asian scraping technique [3].

Within a looks-oriented wiki its relevance is mostly indirect: practitioners describe it as a way to feel better and more energetic, and its cousin facial gua sha has been promoted by beauty influencers for lymphatic drainage and skin rejuvenation [3]. Kerokan is traditionally a body treatment rather than a facial one, and the streaks it leaves can be visible for days.

Published research is limited to case reports and qualitative work. A forensic case report documents kerokan-related abrasions, blisters and bruises [1], and a qualitative study notes its use for breast pain among patients who later presented with advanced cancer [2]. Critics of gua sha in general, including Edzard Ernst and Mark Crislip, say it lacks high-quality evidence of clinical benefit [3].

paras: Kerokan involves abrading the skin over various parts of the body with a blunt object such as a coin or a piece of ginger [1]. Oil or balm is applied first and strokes are repeated until reddish marks appear. Gua sha, of which kerokan is the Indonesian name, uses similar one-directional strokes with tools such as ceramic spoons, jade or buffalo horn, and is often paired with cupping [3].

Wikipedia traces gua sha to China, with formal use in traditional Chinese medicine documented from the Ming dynasty (1368-1644), and notes that similar scraping practices exist across Southeast Asia, including Vietnam (cạo gió) and Indonesia [3]. Facial gua sha spread through social media in 2021-2022 [3].

Practitioners associate kerokan with relief from colds, fatigue and body aches; the red streaks are traditionally read as a sign that the ailment is being drawn out. Facial gua sha promoters claim lymphatic drainage and skin rejuvenation [3].

No controlled trials of kerokan for appearance were identified. The literature consists of a forensic case report of a 30-year-old woman whose kerokan-related neck and face abrasions raised suspicion of assault before an autopsy found myocarditis as the cause of death [1], and a qualitative study in which most Indonesian breast cancer patients interviewed used kerokan and a traditional drink for breast pain before diagnosis at an advanced stage [2].

Gua sha nearly always causes minor skin trauma such as redness, bruising or dermatitis; burns and blood in the urine have been reported, and rare serious cases including cerebral hemorrhage and injuries requiring skin grafts appear in the literature [3]. Infection is a concern with unsterilized tools or broken skin [3]. Authors of the forensic report stress that clinicians and investigators should recognise such marks as the result of a cultural practice [1]. Wikipedia also records fears among Vietnamese immigrants in the 1980s that marks from the similar cạo gió would be reported as child abuse [3].
